extracted.intended_audience: patent classification officers, patent examiners, patent information professionals, and users of the IPC (e.g., searchers and applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and guidance for classifying and presenting patent documents under the International Patent Classification (IPC), including the hierarchical structure, symbols, references, Definitions and supplementary material used to guide classification and searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of the IPC
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification's primary purpose is to establish an effective search tool for retrieval of patent documents to establish novelty and evaluate inventive step or non-obviousness (including assessment of technical advance and useful results or utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional purposes: (a) orderly arrangement of patent documents to facilitate access to technological and legal information; (b) basis for selective dissemination of information; (c) basis for investigating the state of the art in given fields; (d) basis for preparation of industrial property statistics to assess technological development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official texts and internet publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification is established in English and French (both authentic) and the Internet version on the WIPO IPC website represents the official publication of the IPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet publication contains the complete text of the edition/version in force and previous editions/versions; communications relating to the Classification should be addressed to WIPO (contact details provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical structure and levels (Section / Class / Subclass / Group / Subgroup)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPC is hierarchical: section (A–H) is highest, then class (section + two digits), subclass (class + capital letter), group (main group or subgroup indicated by numbers and an oblique stroke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main group symbols end with '/00'; subgroup numbers are decimals of main-group numbers; subgroup titles are indented and read as dependent on higher-level titles; a complete classification symbol combines section, class, subclass and main group/subgroup (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of hierarchy (dots/indentation govern hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hierarchy among subgroups is determined solely by the number of dots (indentation) preceding their titles, not by the numbering of the subgroups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dots preceding group titles may substitute for repeated words of superior groups; examples show how multi-dot subgroup titles are to be read as increasingly specific subdivisions of parent groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to classify in main groups only
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial property offices lacking sufficient expertise may classify patent documents in main groups only (i.e., not to detailed subgrouping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an accepted option to reflect limited classification resources or expertise; main-group-only classification still valid for core search/representation needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of groups within a subclass
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups in each subclass are arranged in a sequence to assist the user; newer subclasses generally order main groups from most complex/highly specialised to least complex/least specialised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Residual main groups (e.g., 99/00) are placed at the end of schemes where needed; the arrangement follows a standardised sequence from complex to less complex subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance headings
rubrics_metrics.description: When successive main groups relate to common subject matter, a short underlined 'guidance heading' may precede the first such main group to indicate the common subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A guidance heading covers the series of groups up to the next guidance heading or to a heavy type line used to separate different subject matter; in exceptional cases, a guidance heading may cover a single main group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of titles (single-part, multipart, semicolon conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles may use a single phrase or several related phrases linked together; multipart titles separated by semicolons each constitute separate titles and should be interpreted independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multipart titles are used when it is desirable to treat distinct kinds of subject matter together that cannot be covered by a single phrase (examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: References — functions and types
rubrics_metrics.description: References in titles/notes point to other places in the IPC and have functions: limiting references (scope-limitation, precedence) and non-limiting references (application-oriented, out of residual place, informative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting references exclude specified subject matter from the place where they appear and indicate where that subject matter is classified; precedence references resolve overlapping/classifiable-in-two-places issues. Non-limiting references indicate related places of interest for searching but do not change scope. In Definitions, limiting and non-limiting references are listed under specific headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-limitation references (limiting references)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scope-limitation reference specifies subject matter which is taken to another place even though it would otherwise be covered by the title of the place where the reference appears — it excludes specified subject matter and indicates where it is classified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very important for correct use; in Definitions, scope-limitation references appear under 'Limiting references' and use full descriptions of excluded subject matter. Example: A47B 25/00 excludes billiard tables which are classified in A63D 15/00.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedence references (limiting references)
rubrics_metrics.description: A precedence reference states that another place 'takes precedence' when subject matter is classifiable in two places or when different aspects are covered by different places and it is desired that it be classified in only one place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedence references can function as scope-limitation references or as classification rules for combination-type subject matter depending on the relationship between affected places; they are often used at subgroup level and may be replaced by a higher-level note when several groups are affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting references: application-oriented, residual-place, informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting references point to places relevant for special adaptation/use/incorporation (application-oriented), point out places covering subject matter from residual places (references out of residual places), or indicate locations of subject matter of interest for searching though outside the scope (informative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting references are being moved from schemes into Definitions to keep schemes readable; examples show typical application-oriented and informative references (e.g., lasers -> eye surgery A61F /* etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and interpretation of references (placement and punctuation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: References are usually placed at the end of the title part to which they relate; references following a subclass/group title relate to all hierarchically inferior places; when multiple items refer to same place, separate with commas and give the symbol only once; when items refer to different places, separate references with semicolons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A quoted group is usually the most relevant but not necessarily the only relevant group; hierarchical relations of quoted groups should also be considered; examples illustrate comma vs semicolon use and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes (definition and overriding effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes define or explain specific words/phrases or indicate how subject matter is classified; notes may be associated with sections, subsections, classes, subclasses or groups and apply only to the places concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes override any general guidance in case of conflict (e.g., a Note following a subclass title overrides a Note following the section title); information in higher-level notes is also provided within subclass Definitions for impacted places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of cited classification symbols (inclusion of inferior subdivisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a symbol or contiguous range of symbols is cited in a title, reference or note, the citation comprises not just the symbol(s) explicitly mentioned but their full range of hierarchically inferior subdivisions as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IPC therefore does not use expressions like '... class and its subclasses ...' because a cited subclass implicitly includes its main groups and subgroups; when indicating intervals, the end is identified by the hierarchically highest symbol that covers the last intended group without incorporating unintended groups; non-contiguous ranges must cite each block separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indication of changes relative to previous editions/versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes are signalled in the text so users can see what is new, changed, or deleted: italics mean new/changed/file-scope-changed or deleted; italics are followed by version indicators in square brackets (e.g., [4] or [2008.01]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deleted group symbols appear with an italic indication of where the subject matter is transferred to in the current edition/version; multiple version indicators may be associated with an entry (only last shown by default).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary information: Definitions, Non-limiting references, Chemical formulae and graphic illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPC includes supplementary data accessible via the Internet publication: Definitions (clarify boundaries of classification places but do not change scope), non-limiting references introduced into Definitions to aid searching, chemical structural formulae and graphical illustrations where needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions follow a structured format with a definition statement, explanation of limiting and informative references, interpretation of special classifying rules and definitions of terms; chemical formulae are included in schemes only when necessary to define scope and more extensively in Definitions as illustrative examples; graphic illustrations are used similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard expressions and terminology (covered/provided for, residual, combination, logical connectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardised wording and meanings used throughout the IPC: e.g., 'covered' or 'provided for' mean subject matter can be classified in that place; 'not otherwise provided for' means not provided for in any other group in the same subclass or any other subclass; special meanings for 'i.e.' (equals), 'e.g.' (illustrative), 'A and B', 'A or B', 'either A or B, but not both'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressions signalling combination subject matter ('… covered by more than one of main groups …') indicate that only combinations of characteristics falling within multiple groups are covered; examples provided; interpret 'e.g.' as inclusion but non-limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: File scope of a group
rubrics_metrics.description: The file scope of a group is the subject matter that falls within the scope of a group and is not specified in any subgroup indented thereunder; for a group with no subgroups the scope and file scope are identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When new subgroups are added to a group, its scope remains unchanged but its file scope is reduced (i.e., residual subject matter remains in the parent group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention information and inventive thing (definitions for classification purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Invention information’ is all novel and unobvious subject matter in a patent document (description, drawings, claims) that represents an addition to the state of the art; an 'inventive thing' is any part of the invention information which is novel and unobvious in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invention information should usually be determined using the claims of the patent document for guidance; these definitions inform what must be represented by classification (see also 'obligatory classification').

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligatory classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification necessary to completely represent the invention information of a patent document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligatory classification indicates which places are needed to fully represent the technical and novel aspects of the document; use Definitions and scope rules to determine obligatory places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary and technical-term guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A glossary of technical terms and expressions used in the Classification explains meanings when terms have alternative meanings or are used more precisely/restrictively than common usage; definitions in the Classification override the Glossary for affected places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guide provides definitions for many technical expressions (e.g., apparatus, arrangement, genus/species, combination/subcombination, residual place, plant, product, treatment, variable) and instructs that the meaning should be considered in technical context with examples illustrating usage.
